flashcards.front: What three mathematical properties must CRDT merge functions satisfy to converge identically without locks?
flashcards.back: Associativity, Commutativity, and Idempotence—ensuring any peer network can deliver, reorder, or duplicate deltas across offline partitions and still reach identical final state.

flashcards.front: Contrast Local (Document-Partitioned) vs Global (Term-Partitioned) secondary indexes.
flashcards.back: Local indexes give fast single-shard atomic writes but require scatter-gather reads across ALL shards (p99 hit); Global indexes give O(1) fast shard reads at the cost of async cross-shard write updates.

quizzes.scenario: Editors in Tokyo and London lose their connection for 10 minutes, edit overlapping paragraphs offline, then reconnect.
quizzes.question: Which approach merges both sides with no lost keystrokes and no central lock?
options: A central lock on each paragraph that offline users must hold
Sequence CRDT operations merged on reconnect
Last-write-wins on each paragraph, by wall-clock time
Keep both versions and ask the users to merge them manually
quizzes.explanation: Sequence CRDTs give each insert a unique position id (for example a counter plus peer id), and merging is commutative and idempotent, so every replica converges to the same text. Last-write-wins discards one side's edits.
optionExplanations: Offline editors cannot reach the lock, so they could not edit.
Correct. Every replica converges and keeps both sets of edits.
One side's paragraph edits are thrown away, and clocks can skew.
This avoids loss but pushes merge work onto every user.

quizzes.scenario: Document storage grows from 8 to 16 nodes, and workspace dashboards search documents by tag.
quizzes.question: Which layout avoids rehashing every key and avoids querying all nodes for each tag search?
options: hash(doc_id) % N with a local tag index on each node
Replicate every document to all 16 nodes for fast search
Range sharding by creation time with a local tag index
Fixed logical buckets that move whole, plus a global tag index
quizzes.explanation: Map documents to a fixed number of logical buckets and move whole buckets when nodes join, so most keys stay put. A global tag index, updated asynchronously, answers tag searches from one place; a session token can make readers wait until their own recent writes are indexed.
optionExplanations: Changing N rehashes most keys, and local indexes need scatter-gather.
Full replication multiplies storage and write cost by 16.
New documents hotspot the newest range, and tags still scatter.
Correct. Few keys move, and tag search reads one index.
